title: Extension planning, concurrency surge & data sovereignty sync
summary: Quarterly renewal/extension discussion focused on adding reserved capacity for spike concurrency, gating EU data sovereignty (onprem/VPC), and aligning SLA/latency expectations. Redwood AE/SE pair outlined Dedicated vs Hosted fallbacks, brief benchmark plan, and security attachments to send. Agreed next step: pilot configuration doc, security pack, pricing amendment, and a kickoff for a benchmark run week of Dec 6.
topics:
1) Current usage patterns and headroom (concurrency spikes)
2) Options for reserved capacity and burst choreography
3) EU data residency/VPC/onprem requirements and KMS integration
4) Latency SLOs and canary rollout strategy
5) Pricing amendment & contract extension timeline
action_items: Olivia Chen: send pricing amendment and contract mark-up by 2026-12-02
Marcus Li: share pilot benchmark spreadsheet + suggested payloads by 2026-12-03
Lena Rhee: provide list of compliance docs required (SOC2 scopes, encryption at rest regs) by 2026-12-01
James Ortega: confirm internal test window for benchmarking (Dec 6-10) by 2026-12-01
next_steps: Send security pack (SOC2 summary, KMS integration guide, VPC networking notes)
Share dedicated capacity sizing recommendation + burst choreography options
Schedule 2-hr benchmark kickoff and run (Dec 6-10 tentative)
Draft contract amendment with extension term and reserved GPU units
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-29 16:00 UTC | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Olivia, Marcus (Redwood); Sophie, James, Lena, Tom (Arboretum)

[00:00] Olivia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Friday afternoon, appreciate it. We're here to run through the extension planning and the concurrency/burst and data sovereignty items.
[00:12] Sophie: Yeah thanks, Olivia, quick context — we do have an existing Dedicated pool with Redwood, used for customer-facing chat and internal summarization tasks. Over the last two quarters we've seen a few production spikes and we want to avoid throttling during close-of-day batch flows.
[00:28] Marcus: got it, and when you say spikes, is that sustained QPS for a few minutes or very short high bursts?
[00:33] James: it's more like 3-8 minute bursts during our settlement windows, sometimes simultaneous queries across multiple services so effective concurrency goes up to about 220 concurrent tokens-gen/cardinality.
[00:44] Olivia: okay that's helpful. Current committed capacity is 180 concurrent units, so short of that. there are two levers — increase reserved capacity or configure burst overlay (ephemeral hosts) plus routing policy. both have trade offs on cost and latency.
[01:01] Tom: cost is a big part, we want predictable billing but also need to avoid user-facing latency regressions. can we do a canary with auto-fallback to hosted during big spikes?
[01:10] Marcus: yes, Redwood supports routing policies. typical pattern: primary Dedicated, canary rollout to a bigger instance type, and fallback to Hosted with rate limiting control. we showed a similar flow with BetaBank last quarter. latency differences depend on model variant and region.
[01:26] Sophie: EU residency is a hard requirement for some datasets — anything involving EU customer PII must stay in-region. we're evaluating VPC/private deployment options for that subset. what are the options again?
[01:36] Marcus: three main options: 1) Hosted EU with data residency controls and contractual residency (fastest), 2) Dedicated in EU region with private VPC peering (middle), 3) Private on-prem appliance (longest lead but full control). for KMS, we support customer-managed keys via standard KMS/HSM integrations. note: some of our docs have 'KSM' typo in one place so we'll send corrected guide.
[01:56] Lena: just to be clear, we need audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and proof of data at rest encryption with our key material — SOC2 attestation not just a summary.
[02:07] Olivia: completely reasonable. We'll attach the SOC2 report PDF and the KMS integration guide. Marcus will include the audit log retention options in the security pack.
[02:16] James: for the burst plan, how quickly can you spin up the overlay nodes in EU? we need < 90s cold start ideally for traffic routed to hosted fallback.
[02:26] Marcus: cold-start depends on image caching and instance type; typical warm-up is ~60-120s for smallest GPU profiles, 30-60s for larger warm pools. we recommend a small warm standby that auto-expands — the concurrency controller uses historical sequence length distributions to size batches efficiently.
[02:44] Speaker 1: sorry, can I ask about tokenization and cost — are you able to suggest quantization to reduce cost without impacting quality?
[02:51] Marcus: yeah, we have quantization recommendations — Q4 quant profiles are model specific. for your summarization payloads, int8/q4h is often a sweet spot; Marcus: (laughs) sorry my voice overlapped.
[03:03] Tom: we've experimented with internal optimizations but concerned about hallucination risk when quantizing. how does Redwood help monitor quality regressions?
[03:12] Olivia: Redwood Optimize does model/regression monitoring tied to prompt sets. we can wire in your canonical prompt test suite and set alerts for BLEU/ROUGE/LLM-specific quality metrics; if quality dips after quantization or model change we can auto-fallback to a higher-precision variant.
[03:29] Sophie: timeline wise — we want a contract extension to cover next 12 months plus the reserved top-up effective Jan 1. is that feasible?
[03:36] Olivia: yes, typical timeline: we'll draft amendment this week, get legal review, and aim for signature mid-December to make Jan 1 effective. we'll also include the burst credits and a clause for a one-time benchmarking window.
[03:47] Lena: legal will need the encryption at rest proof and the KMS flow diagram for our internal audit.
[03:53] Olivia: noted. Marcus will send architecture diagram with KMS and VPC peering notes.
[03:58] James: for benchmarking, we want to run a throughput + latency sim with production-like payloads. can Redwood run the load or do we need to provide runners?
[04:06] Marcus: we can coordinate — usually customers run their load against our staging endpoints, we provide traffic templates, and we'll instrument token-level latency and per-route traces. suggest 2-hour warmup + 2-hour run plus a separate smaller canary run.
[04:21] Tom: ok makes sense. are there any limits on how many canaries/variants we can create?
[04:27] Marcus: no hard limit, but policy complexity increases operationally. we recommend a simple A/B with fallback chain: Dedicated (v1) -> Dedicated (v2 higher concurrency) -> Hosted region EU fallback.
[04:39] Sophie: what about failover across regions? we can't send EU PII to non-EU fallback. can you route only non-PII traffic to global fallback?
[04:48] Olivia: yes, routing rules can be tag-based — you can tag requests as 'sensitive' and Redwood will only route tagged requests to in-region capacity. untagged traffic can fall back globally. small caveat: tagging must be enforced at app layer.
[05:02] Lena: great. one more thing — can we do a short PoC for onprem containerized serving? we want to measure throughput with our internal accelerators.
[05:10] Marcus: onprem pilots are possible; lead time is usually 6-10 weeks for an appliance-style deploy, shorter for VPC private deployments. we'll scope a lightweight onprem pilot (no HSM first) to validate throughput then plan KMS/attestation next.
[05:25] Sophie: cost question: if we commit to extra reserved units, do we get priority for capacity during bursts?
[05:31] Olivia: reserved units give you prioritization in Dedicated pools and predictable throughput. burst overlay can be configured to use reserved burst credits first, then billed overage if the burst exceeds credits. we can provide a cost model in the amendment.
[05:46] James: regarding SLAs — our product requires p50 < 150ms for 512 token responses in EU region, is that realistic at your end?
[05:55] Marcus: p50 150ms is aggressive depending on model size; for medium LLMs with optimized kernels and short sequences it's achievable in Dedicated EU local, but for longer sequences p50 may creep. we'll run benchmarking with your 512-token payload to validate. if not met we can propose a performance tier.
[06:13] Tom: can we add a clause for remediation if SLO missed during a month? credits or rollback?
[06:18] Olivia: yes, standard SLA credits and an escalation path — we'll include our remediation policy in the contract amendment.
[06:24] Sophie: can you clarify network egress and peering costs? we have concerns about cross-AZ egress.
[06:30] Marcus: peering reduces egress costs but depends on cloud network topology. for VPC peering we recommend colocated instances in the same AZ where possible. we'll include a network guidance note with estimates.
[06:41] Speaker 2: (muffled) also curious about audit log retention — do you keep raw transcripts by default?
[06:48] Lena: we need to ensure transcripts of EU PII aren't stored outside EU.
[06:52] Olivia: default retention is 30 days but configurable; for sensitive traffic we can set in-region-only retention and shorter retention windows, with options to disable transcript retention. we'll include the retention APIs in the pack.
[07:05] Sophie: ok let's recap — you're gonna send the amendment, security pack (SOC2 + KMS + retention), benchmark templates, and schedule the benchmark window for Dec 6-10.
[07:13] Olivia: correct. Marcus: i'll share the pilot spreadsheet and the architecture diagram.
[07:18] James: i'll confirm the internal test window and the list of payloads we want to run.
[07:22] Tom: legal will review once amendment is in.
[07:25] Olivia: great — any other blockers?
[07:28] Lena: just one ask — can you include a list of Redwood's partner clouds by region? helps our compliance folks map endpoints.
[07:34] Marcus: yes, will include a matrix of cloud partners and region mapping.
[07:38] Olivia: perfect. thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and get that benchmark scheduled.
[07:43] [END]
